text: Routing an alert to the right person, at the right urgency, without burning out whoever's on call, is its own discipline, separate from building the dashboard that fires the alert in the first place. This lesson covers severity, routing, and the concrete practices that keep a rotation sustainable instead of exhausting.

A workable severity model usually has three tiers. Sev1 is a customer-facing outage — page immediately, any hour. Sev2 is degraded but not fully down — page during business hours, or escalate if nobody acknowledges it. Sev3 is worth knowing about, so it becomes a ticket or a Slack message, never a page. Route everything through one queue at Sev1 urgency instead, and a flood of low-severity noise teaches the on-call engineer to ignore pages — the opposite of what alerting exists to do.

The second failure mode is routing every alert to one generic rotation no matter which service actually broke, which wastes the time of someone who can't act on it. The fix is label-based routing: every alert carries labels for service, team, and severity, and Alertmanager's routing tree matches on those labels. A critical alert labeled team equals payments reaches the payments team's pager through its own matched route — never the checkout team, which has its own separate route.

Two more mechanics in that same config keep the rotation from drowning. group_by on alertname and service is deduplication — many firing alerts for one root cause collapse into a single notification instead of one page per affected instance. And inhibit_rules suppress a HighLatency alert automatically once a ServiceDown alert for that same service is already firing, because once a service is fully down, a stream of latency alerts for the same outage is noise, not new information.

One more practice doesn't come from the alert data at all: a silence. Before a planned deploy or maintenance window, someone creates a time-bounded rule muting everything matching a given service for the next couple of hours, so expected noise during known work never pages anyone. That's the difference worth remembering — inhibition is automatic, based on another alert already firing; a silence is a human decision made ahead of time.

Severity decides urgency, labels decide who gets paged, and deduplication, grouping, and silences keep the volume survivable. Next, once the right page reaches the right person, it needs to hand them something more useful than just the words 'service is down' — that's what a real runbook does.
